title: Corneal epithelial cell
summary: The living cells of the cornea's outer skin, in a stack five to seven deep: flat on top, many-sided in the middle, tall at the bottom.

layers.basics: The front of the eye is covered by a skin of clear cells only about 50 micrometres thick. The cells are alive and see-through. The ones at the very top are wide flat plates washed by tears. Under them lie wing cells, and at the bottom a single row of tall basal cells divides to replace the ones lost above. A cell is shed about a week to ten days after it is made.
layers.deeper: Each kind is built for its place. Surface cells are 40 to 60 micrometres across and only a few micrometres thick, their tops folded into small ridges and fingers that hold the tear film, and their sides sealed against the tears. Wing cells are many-sided and packed with keratin bundles that end at desmosomes on their sides. Basal cells are columns about 20 micrometres tall that grip the basement membrane below with hemidesmosomes. Unlike skin, the surface cells are not dead scales.
layers.expert: The drawing of this card shows one wing cell; the surface cell and the basal cell have drawings of their own. The wing cell's width and height come from confocal measurements of the central cornea; the nucleus size and small organelles are illustrative. New cells come from stem cells at the rim of the cornea as well as from the basal row.

open_questions: Confocal gives a 12.7 µm basal layer against about 20 µm in histology: which is closer to the living cell?

title: Corneal surface cell
summary: The top cells of the cornea's outer skin: wide, thin, living plates whose ridged tops hold the tear film.

layers.basics: The very top of the eye's clear front is a layer of flat cells, each a thin plate about 50 micrometres across and only a few micrometres thick. They are alive and see-through. Tears wash over them, and they are shed into the tears about a week to ten days after they are made.
layers.deeper: Their tops are folded into low winding ridges, microplicae, with a few short microvilli among them. These hold the inner, mucus layer of the tear film so that the tears spread over the eye. The sides of neighbouring surface cells are sealed with tight junctions, so tears cannot seep between them, and desmosomes tie them together.
layers.expert: Measured in human eyes: 40 to 60 µm across and 2 to 6 µm thick, with flattened nuclei. The drawing is 50 µm across and 4 µm thick; the spacing and height of the ridges and the numbers of microvilli and organelles are illustrative. The tight junctions and the tear film are not drawn.

title: Corneal basal cell
summary: The bottom row of the cornea's outer skin: tall columns, riveted to the layer below, and the only cells of the stack that divide.

layers.basics: At the bottom of the cornea's clear skin stands a single row of tall cells. They hold on to the thin sheet beneath them and divide to make new cells, which move up the stack and are shed at the top a week or so later.
layers.deeper: Each basal cell is a column about 20 micrometres tall in stained sections, fixed to the basement membrane below by hemidesmosomes and to its neighbours by desmosomes, with keratin bundles running between them inside. When the hemidesmosomes hold badly the skin can lift off, which hurts.
layers.expert: Measured in human eyes: about 20 µm tall in histology, 12.8 µm across by confocal microscopy (which gives a thinner basal layer, 12.7 µm, than histology does). The basement membrane is 40 to 60 nm thick and is drawn far thicker so that it shows. The nucleus size and the numbers of junctions and organelles are illustrative.

facts: yes, the only layer that does
open_questions: Confocal gives a 12.7 µm basal layer against about 20 µm in histology: which is closer to the living cell?

title: Junctions of the corneal epithelium
summary: The ties between corneal cells: desmosomes along the sides, tight seals near the top, and hemidesmosomes at the base.

layers.basics: Cells of the cornea's skin hold on to each other and to the layer below. Along their sides are desmosomes, small protein rivets. Near the top, the sides of the surface cells are sealed so tears cannot seep between them. At the bottom, the tall cells are fixed to the layer beneath by hemidesmosomes, half-rivets.
layers.deeper: A desmosome links the keratin bundles of one cell to those of the next, so a push on one cell is spread over many. The seals near the surface keep tears out of the gaps between cells. Hemidesmosomes anchor the lowest cells to the basement membrane; when they fail, the skin can lift and the eye hurts, as in recurrent corneal erosion.
layers.expert: Reviews differ on which junction sits where: one places the tight seals only on the sides of the topmost cells, another gives wing cells similar seals. Only the desmosomes are drawn, 120 in the model, an illustrative number.

facts: along the sides of all cells
near the surface; some reviews also place them between wing cells
open_questions: Which layers carry full tight junctions in the living human cornea?
